A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LATINO-PRO work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original restoration experiments on FFHQ and AFHQ, including deblurring, super-resolution, and inpainting, plus appendix ablations and Food-101 examples.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds phase-retrieval examples, sensitivity analyses, and an SDXL-based comparison.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and the core stochastic-autoencoder and prompt-optimization procedures remain unchanged. New Appendix E extends the proximal step to nonlinear operators through an Adam-based least-squares solve, providing a limited procedural adaptation.

E1.justification: v2 adds nonlinear Fourier-magnitude phase retrieval on FFHQ-512, illustrated by two examples in Figure 9. The existing FFHQ, AFHQ, Food-101, deblurring, super-resolution, inpainting, and difficult-noise coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The existing comparator methods remain represented, including P2L, TReg, LDPS, PSLD, and LDIR. Added experiments reuse existing methods under new tasks or backbone settings; the newly cited consistency-model approaches are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands the evaluation design with step-size sweeps, three prompt initializations, SDXL baseline comparisons at 50 and 1000 steps, and nonlinear reconstruction using 300 Adam iterations. Appendix J also changes P2L/TReg efficiency benchmarking from published figures and pseudocode-based implementations to official-code-based implementations. The original restoration benchmark protocols remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds distinct analyses of step-size sensitivity (Appendix B, Figures 6–7), prompt wording (Appendix F, Table 5), and whether stronger priors explain performance (Appendix G, Figure 11). These substantially extend the existing prior-choice, prompt-tuning, and difficult-case analyses.

E5.justification: New Figure 7 explicitly reports moving-average smoothing with window 3 for its sensitivity curves. The existing 20-seed prompt-optimization analysis and shaded bands are retained as Figure 20; no increased run count or new significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–2 and the retained restoration tables preserve their scores, but baseline resource results are substantially replaced: P2L changes from approximately 10.6 GB and 600 s to 8.18 GB and 402 s; P2L-XL changes from approximately 43.3 GB and 3122 s to 57.1 GB and 6800 s. These reflect revised benchmarking, not same-setting performance gains. New sensitivity, prompt, SDXL, and phase-retrieval results also expand the evidence.

T1.justification: Equation 4 gains the missing initial-state term x_k before the Langevin increment, correcting the stated discretization. The existing gradient derivation and Proposition 1 proof are retained. New Appendix C mainly explains the existing formulation and convergence expectations rather than proving a new theorem.

C1.justification: The introduction acknowledges concurrent consistency-model inverse solvers and qualifies the remaining research gap around high-resolution latent models with prompt conditioning. The principal LATINO/LATINO-PRO contributions, 8/68-NFE claims, and concluding performance claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: New Appendix C distinguishes Langevin time from diffusion time, explains the clean-image likelihood advantage, and qualifies expected small-t convergence while leaving large-t analysis open. New ablation discussions interpret prompt robustness and prior-backbone effects. Existing limitations concerning strong noise and misleading prompts remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access pointer in the abstract, nonlinear-solver settings including Adam learning rate 0.001 and 300 iterations, official baseline-code provenance, and precision-related implementation explanations. These extend the already detailed implementation information; the PDFs alone do not verify the linked code's availability.

R1.justification: v2 adds concurrent consistency-model work by Garber and Tirer, Li et al., and Xu et al., qualifying its novelty positioning. It also cites Blanes et al. on splitting methods. Most related-work discussion and existing references are retained.

P1.justification: Most prose remains intact. v2 locally revises the introduction and method explanation, moves references before the separately numbered supplementary material, inserts three appendix sections, and updates affiliations and acknowledgments. This is a limited reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds sensitivity Figures 6–7, phase-retrieval Figure 9, SDXL comparison Figure 11, and prompt-ablation Table 5. Existing displays are largely preserved, with local relocation and resizing, including the final inpainting and difficult-case figures.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens validation through sensitivity tests and a prior-backbone control, corrects Equation 4, and improves implementation and benchmarking documentation while retaining earlier evidence. The gains are limited by the mainly illustrative nonlinear/SDXL comparisons. Table 5 also leaves evaluation resolution unclear: its FFHQ-1024 caption accompanies default-prompt scores matching the FFHQ-512 results in Table 2.
